description: Hi everyone! We are a team of three who are excited to take part in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Two of our team members are siblings studying in Year 7, and they love solving problems and coming up with new ideas. Our third teammate joined us after we met at an event, and she enjoys coding and app development
summary:
Project Summary
Space exploration presents challenges beyond travelling through the universe. Astronauts on long-duration missions must manage demanding schedules, physical health, sleep routines, mental wellbeing and unexpected mission situations while operating far away from Earth.
NOVA (Astronaut Health & Mission Companion) is a student-designed digital prototype that explores how technology can support astronaut health awareness and everyday wellbeing during space missions.

The platform brings together four key features: a personalised daily routine planner, a wellbeing check-in, interactive educational activities and mission-based emergency awareness simulations. Astronauts can explore a sample daily schedule, record their mood and energy levels, practice healthy habits and learn how to respond appropriately to simulated situations such as oxygen-system alerts and radiation exposure.
NOVA aims to make astronaut well-being easier to understand through a simple, interactive, and accessible interface. It also demonstrates how digital tools could support structured routines, self-awareness, and mission preparedness during long-duration space exploration. Future development could explore integration with wearable sensors, expert-reviewed health protocols, and secure astronaut health data.
Our vision: To make astronaut well-being an essential part of humanity's journey towards longer and safer space missions.
details:
NOVA – Astronaut Health & Mission Companion

NOVA is a student-designed digital platform concept created to explore how technology can support astronauts' physical and mental wellbeing during long-duration space missions.

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Life in space is challenging. Astronauts experience demanding work schedules, changes in sleep patterns, limited opportunities for exercise, isolation from family and Earth, and exposure to environmental hazards.

NOVA addresses these challenges through four interactive features:

  • Daily Routine Planner: Allows users to explore a sample astronaut schedule that includes work, exercise, meals and rest.
  • Wellbeing Check-in: Provides a simple way to record mood and energy levels and encourages reflection on personal wellbeing.
  • Mission Scenario Simulator: Introduces educational situations such as oxygen-system alerts and radiation exposure, allowing users to explore appropriate decisions.
  • Interactive Learning: Encourages users to understand space-related challenges through activities and scenario-based learning.

The website follows a simple three-step journey: set up a sample profile, plan and check in, and learn through mission scenarios.

2. What benefits does it have?

NOVA demonstrates how a digital companion could make astronaut wellbeing more organised, understandable and engaging.

Its potential benefits include:

  • Encouraging balanced daily routines involving exercise, meals, work and rest.
  • Promoting awareness of mental wellbeing during isolation and confinement.
  • Helping astronauts and learners understand environmental challenges in space.
  • Encouraging mission preparedness through interactive educational scenarios.
  • Presenting complex space-health concepts through a simple and accessible interface.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our long-term vision is to contribute to the conversation around astronaut wellbeing during extended space missions, including future missions to the Moon and Mars.

We want to highlight that successful space exploration is not only about spacecraft, technology, and reaching new destinations; it is also about supporting the people who undertake these missions.

NOVA demonstrates an approach that could be expanded into a more advanced astronaut well-being platform through future integration with wearable sensors, secure health-data systems, and expert-reviewed health protocols.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We developed NOVA as a browser-based interactive website using:

  • HTML5: To structure the website and its content.
  • CSS3: To design the interface, layouts, colours and responsive experience.
  • JavaScript: To develop interactive features, sample routine planning, wellbeing check-ins and mission scenarios.
  • Web Browser: To run and test the working prototype.
  • Netlify: Intended for public website hosting and accessibility.

The current prototype is software-based and does not require external hardware. It does not currently connect to wearable sensors, collect live astronaut health data or use real-time AI analysis.

5. How is your project creative?

NOVA combines astronaut well-being awareness with interactive learning in one simple digital experience.

Instead of presenting space-health information as static text, we created a platform where users can explore routines, reflect on well-being, and make decisions in simulated mission situations.

One creative aspect is the use of situation-based learning. For example, users can explore what an oxygen-system alert or radiation-related situation means and learn why following mission-approved procedures and communicating with the crew are important.

We also focused on making the experience visually engaging and easy to understand, even for people who are not familiar with space science or astronaut health.

6. What factors did your team consider?

During the development of NOVA, we considered several important factors:

  • Physical well-being: The importance of exercise, meals, rest, and structured routines.
  • Mental well-being: The effects of isolation, confinement, and separation from Earth.
  • Space environment: Awareness of radiation and oxygen-system-related risks.
  • Usability: Making the platform simple, engaging, and accessible.
  • Mission safety: Ensuring that educational scenarios encourage following approved mission procedures rather than suggesting unverified emergency instructions.
  • Future scalability: Exploring how the concept could eventually connect with real monitoring technologies and expert-reviewed systems.
  • Data responsibility: Recognizing the importance of privacy and secure handling of sensitive astronaut health information.
